Connacht
KON-akht
n. (the western Irish province to which the Cromwellian settlement transplanted the dispossessed Catholic landowners after 1654)
Irish Connacht, the descendants of Conn, from the legendary Conn Cétchathach; the anglicised form Connaught is also used.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Connacht is the western province of Ireland, comprising Galway, Mayo, Sligo, Roscommon and Leitrim, the poorest and most Irish-speaking of the four. Its place in the dictionary is the Cromwellian settlement. After the reconquest of 1649 to 1653, the Act for the Settling of Ireland and the Act of Satisfaction provided that the estates of Catholic landowners judged to have been in rebellion should be forfeited, that the soldiers and the adventurers who had financed the war should be paid in Irish land, and that such proprietors as were allowed any land at all should receive it in Connacht and Clare, west of the Shannon. Some two thousand families were ordered to transplant by May 1654. The phrase to Hell or Connaught preserves what the transaction looked like to those subjected to it. The province afterwards held a dense Irish-speaking population on poor ground, and the famine of the eighteen-forties fell on it harder than on any other part of Ireland. The dictionary records the transplantation as confiscation under statute and names it so.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to transplant as to remove and plant elsewhere; forfeiture as the loss of property by offence; an adventurer as one who hazards his money; to confiscate as to adjudge to the public treasury; and an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor.

expand to see more

TRANSPLANT, v.t. To remove and plant in another place; to remove and settle or establish for residence.

FORFEITURE, n. The act of forfeiting; the loss of some right, estate or honour, by an offence or crime.

ADVENTURER, n. One who hazards a chance; one who ventures his money in a hazardous enterprise.

CONFISCATE, v.t. To adjudge to be forfeited to the public treasury, as the goods of a criminal.

INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a permanent possession.

Modern Corruption

Western Irish province to which the Cromwellian Act of Satisfaction ordered some two thousand dispossessed Catholic landowning families to transplant by May 1654, their estates going to soldiers and adventurers.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is confiscation by statute, and the dictionary names it against a regime many Reformed readers admire. Cromwell's settlement of Ireland was not a riot; it was legislation, with commissioners, surveys, qualifications and a deadline, under which the land of a nation changed hands to pay an army and its creditors. Naboth's refusal states what a family holding is and why no price makes the transfer lawful: “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3). Ahab proceeded by a legal form too, and the psalmist's name for government conducted that way is the sharpest in Scripture: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20).

The second paragraph distinguishes the two kinds of going out, because Scripture does, and the distinction is the heart of the objection. Abraham was called to leave, and the call came from God with a promise attached: “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1). A family ordered across the Shannon by commissioners under penalty has received no such call and been given no such promise; it has been robbed, and the dictionary will not dress the one in the language of the other. The requirement on every government, Protestant or otherwise, is stated once and is not negotiable: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The dictionary adds that the province so filled was the one the famine of the eighteen-forties afterwards emptied, and that the connection between poor land densely settled by compulsion and a catastrophe two centuries later is not an accident of weather.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Hebrew 'amal (H5999), mischief; Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy.

expand to see more

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage, a possession; “the inheritance of my fathers”, 1 Kings 21:3.

Hebrew chalilah (H2486) — far be it, God forbid; “The LORD forbid it me”, 1 Kings 21:3.

Hebrew 'amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, mischief; “which frameth mischief by a law”, Psalm 94:20.

Hebrew kisse' (H3678) — a seat, a throne; “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee”, Psalm 94:20.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, kindness, steadfast love; “and to love mercy”, Micah 6:8.

Usage

"“the inheritance of my fathers” (1Ki 21:3) — two thousand families ordered to transplant by May 1654."

"“which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20) — commissioners, surveys and a deadline."

"“Get thee out of thy country” (Gen 12:1) — a call with a promise, which this was not."
